title: Jeremy Irons, Keke Palmer, Alan Cumming and More Attached to Projects Launching at Toronto Market
description: Jeremy Irons, Keke Palmer, Alan Cumming and other talent are attached to projects launching at the inaugural market at Toronto Intl. Film Festival,
body:
Jeremy Irons, Keke Palmer, Alan Cumming and other talent are attached to projects launching at the inaugural market at Toronto Intl. Film Festival, known as TIFF: The Market, which runs Sept. 10-16.

	The projects are among 40 film, six series and five “innovation” projects to be pitched at TIFF’s International Financing and Project Market.

	Standout projects include “Central Park Tale,” an animated film produced by Jacqui Barcos and John Fragomeni, and directed by Daniel Jeanette. Among talent attached are Palmer, Cumming, Common and Regina Hall.
	

	Another notable project is “Sher,” which is being produced by David Hamilton, Rajiv Maikhuri and Craig Stovel, and will be directed by Deepa Mehta, with Jeremy Irons attached to star.


	Other well-known names attached to projects include Marlee Matlin, Chase Crawford, Jacob Tremblay and Booker Prize winner Marlon James.

	The full list of projects is here.

	The IFPM is described as a “curated incubator” that aims to accelerate financing and help find co-production and international collaborators for projects. The event, presented by Ontario Creates, brings together more than 50 established producers with financiers, distributors, sales agents and other executives who can help propel their projects worldwide.

	The focus is on content in advanced development, financing and packaging stages. The selected producers will take part in a series of sessions where they will be able to present their projects and network.

	“The projects, the award-winning talent, and the enthusiasm amongst key decision-makers all reflect the emphasis we’ve placed on closing the loop between the ideas and the investments that fuel our global industry,” Charles Tremblay, head of TIFF: The Market, said.

schema.headline: Jeremy Irons, Keke Palmer, Alan Cumming and More Attached to Projects Launching at Toronto Market

title: Locarno Open Doors: Talemwa Pius’ ‘A Vineyard for a Lobster’ and Mohammed Sheikh’s ‘Accept My Plea for a Burial’ Win Top Prizes at Festival’s Africa Industry Focus
description: Ugandan Talemwa Pius’ striking magic realist fable “A Vineyard for a Lobster” and “Accept My Plea for a Burial,” a Somalia set critique of ancient c
body:
Ugandan Talemwa Pius’ striking magic realist fable “A Vineyard for a Lobster” and “Accept My Plea for a Burial,” a Somalia set critique of ancient custom, emerged triumphant at Locarno’s 2026 Open Doors, winning its two biggest cash prizes.

	Neither prize comes as a surprise. 

	Picturing a miraculous snowfall in a drought-ridden Ugandan village, in “A Vineyard for a Lobster,” Pius cleverly spins a political fable of broader collective breakdown, as characters – a desperate trader, a disgraced priest and a reluctant chairman – react to the miracle in self-serving ways rather than thinking about any common good. As their ambitions escalate, the village threatens to fall apart. From Kampala-based Gripmagic, “in the film, an impossible snowfall in a Ugandan village becomes a political allegory, echoing colonial intrusion,” Pius told Variety. 
	

	A €20,000 cash prize was also granted by Open Doors to “Accept My Plea for Burial” (“Baryo Aas Iga Gudoon”), by Mohammed Sheikh a Djibouti, Somalia and Qatar. It kicks in when Warmooge, 12, falls to his death while playing with Waasuge, a fellow goatherd. The village elder fails to resolve the case via customary law and religious counsel. Minnesota-based U.S.-Somali filmmaker Sheik’s follow-up to “Barni,” screening at Locarno, this is “a morally complex story where there is no clear truth, told through a rarely seen Somali cultural framework,” Sheikh told Variety.


	Aseye Fiagbe’s “Too Much Music,” a rehabilitating music doc bio of Kiki Gyan, a Ghanaian keyboard prodigy, took in the same prize. Notably, however, Open Doors prizes announced Aug. 10 at Locarno Pro, the industry zone of Switzerland’s Locarno Film festival, were spread pretty evenly, every single titles among its six project focus walking off with some kind of compensation. 
	

	That prize sweep took in a development grant from France’s CNC national film board for “Chapa 100,” an endearing advanced age love story from Mozambique’s Ique Langa, who impressed with his Rotterdam main competition entry “The Prophet.”

	An ArteKino International Award and a Sørfond Award went to “Tempered Flowers,” a diary-like essay, Tanzania’s Ngelime told Variety. It will use constructed archives, cinema verité performances with her family and stop motion to explore, respectively, Neema’s 1990s childhood, today and imagined future.     

	An EAVE Award was won by Burkina Faso’s Mamounata Nikiema at Pilumpiku Production, a prestigious documentary producer behind multiple doc-features, such as “Djeliya, Memory of Mandingo,” an ambitious, five-county co-pro. 

	“Exploring the lost hope of the Nigerian dream,” “I Live in V.I.,” a social class satire by Ugochukwu Azuya set on Nigeria’s luxurious Victoria Island, won a Tabakalera-San Sebastian residency. The high-energy Adja Soro at the Ivory Coast’s animation-focused Studio KÄ scored an invitation to the Rotterdam Lab.  

	Open Doors 2026 Winners

	Open Doors Grants

	A total of CHF 50,000 ($62,000) sponsored by Visions Sud Est (with the support of the Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation), the City of Bellinzona and the Open Doors initiative.

	“A Vineyard For A Lobster,” by Talemwa Pius, produced by Emmanuel Gashumba (Gripmagic Uganda), Uganda

	CHF 20,000($24,800)

	“Accept My Plea for Burial,” by Mohammed Sheikh, produced by Kadir Harbi (Aleel Films),

	Somalia/Djibouti

	CHF 20,000 ($24,800)

	“Too Much Music,” by Aseye Fiagbe, produced by Aseye Fiagbe (Aseye Fiagbe Creative Studio), Ghana

	CHF10,000 ($12,400) 

	CNC Development Grant

	The CNC development prize is an incentive for the development of a project for the value of €8,000 ($9,200)  

	“Chapa 100,” by Ique Langa, produced by Lara Sousa (Kulunga Filmes), Mozambique

	ArteKino International Award

	Providing an incentive for the development of a project for the value of €6,000 ($6,900). 

	“The Ones with the Tempered Flowers,” by Neema Ngelime, produced by Ivy Kiru (LBx Africa), Tanzania/Kenya
	

	Sørfond Award

	The prize consists in the participation at the Sørfond Pitching Forum at the Films from the South festival for one of the Open Doors Projects, which will be held in November this year in Norway.

	“The Ones with the Tempered Flowers,”

	EAVE Award

	Together with the Film Fund Luxembourg, professional training organisation EAVE will offer a scholarship for the EAVE Marketing Workshop worth €4,000 ($4,600).

	Mamounata Nikiema, (Pilumpiku Production), Burkina FAso

	Tabakalera-San Sebastian Film Festival Residency Award

	The prize consists in a residency in Tabakalera and taking part in the industry activities of the San Sebastian Film Festival, given in collaboration with the International Culture Center Tabakalera and San Sebastian Film Festival.

	“I Live in V.I.,” by Ugochukwu Azuya, produced by Olubunmi Ogunsola at Ensemble, Nigeria

	Rotterdam Lab Award

	In collaboration with IFFR Pro, a participant from the Open Doors Producers will have the chance to take part in the training workshop Rotterdam Lab in January 2027, together with a delegation of more than 70 emerging international producers.

	Adja Mariam Mahre Soro (Studio KÄ), Ivory Coast

	Organisation Internationale de la Francophonie (OIF)

	A consultancy prize to one selected feature film or series project directed by a national of an OIF Member State within the French-speaking Global South, produced or co-produced by a production company based in one of those same Member States.

	“Sarah,” by Pocas Pascoal, Angola

	AFP Critics Prize

	Presented by African Film Press (AFP) LLC, a cross-regional publishing alliance covering the African film, television, and digital media markets. The AFP Critics Prize comprises a $500 cash award, a certificate, and ongoing editorial coverage of the recipient and their future work across AFP’s three founding publications: Akoroko, Sinema Focus, and What Kept Me Up.

	“Submergido,” by Ariel Añez, produced by Joseph Mata, co-produced by Ariel Añez (Maochas Filmes), Mozambique

	The AFP jury 2026 consisted of Kelvin Kariuki (Kenya), Vivian Nwajiaku (Nigeria), Jeffrey Ini-Abasi (Nigeria)

title: A Female Sniper Battles ISIS in First Teaser for Venice Title ‘No Paradise if You Are Killed by a Woman’ (EXCLUSIVE)
description: The fight against the Islamic State has been given the Hollywood-style revenge thriller treatment in Halkawt Mustafa’s “No Paradise if You Are Kille
body:
The fight against the Islamic State has been given the Hollywood-style revenge thriller treatment in Halkawt Mustafa’s “No Paradise if You Are Killed by a Woman,” as revealed by the film’s first teaser trailer. 

	The feature — which will have it world premiere out of competition at the Venice International Film Festival next month — follows a Kurdish-Norwegian female sniper who returns to Mosul in Iraq during the height of ISIS‘ deadly rule, driven by both vengeance and the desperate hope of rescuing her imprisoned younger sister. The teaser features explosions, destruction and deep tensions as the young soldier goes back to the violence she survived, offering a very different narrative retelling of the ISIS story to what’s previously been seen on screen.
	

	“This is a poetic portrait of a woman warrior who refused to bow to darkness,” Mustafa previously told Variety.


	Rising Kurdish star Avan Jamal (“The Exam”) plays the lead, while Norwegian actor Thorbjørn Harr (“The Tunnel,” “22 July”) also stars.

	“No Paradise if You Are Killed by a Woman” marks Kurdish/Norwegian filmmaker Mustafa’s fourth feature film and comes following his 2023 documentary “Hiding Saddam Hussein, delving further into Iraq’s  modern history and exploring how the former president evaded capture following his ousting from power.

	“No Paradise if You Are Killed by a Woman” is also rooted in Mustafa’s own encounters with several women who fought against ISIS, and was inspired by the courage of Nobel Peace Prize laureate and human rights activist Nadia Murad, who was abducted by the terrorist group during the Yazidi genocide of 2014. 
	

	Mustafa wrote and directed “No Paradise if You Are Killed by a Woman” and also produces through his Norway-based Hene Films AS banner, alongside Janne Hjeltnes and John M. Jacobsen. Rome-based sales company True Colours recently boarded the title. 

	See the teaser for “No Paradise if You Are Killed by a Woman” below.

title: Pippa Harris and James Wilson to Headline London Film Festival Industry Forum
description: The BFI London Film Festival has announced that two of the U.K.’s most acclaimed producers will lead the industry program at its upcoming 70th editi
body:
The BFI London Film Festival has announced that two of the U.K.’s most acclaimed producers will lead the industry program at its upcoming 70th edition. 

	Pippa Harris, who produced “Hamnet,” “1917” and is currently working on “The Beatles” biopics, and James Wilson, who produced “The Zone of Interest,” “The Voice of Hind Rajab” and “Under the Skin,” are set to take part in their own spotlight conversations as part of the LFF’s industry forum. 
	

	Harris and Wilson will, according to the festival, discuss their careers, current projects and navigating the international film and TV market in a rapidly changing landscape. 


	“This year our industry programme puts a spotlight on producers and the vital role they play in shepherding artistic visions from their earliest stages through to the screen,” said BFI London Film Festival director Kristy Matheson. “I’m delighted that industry colleagues will have the opportunity to hear from Pippa Harris and James Wilson – two esteemed producers whose unique creative careers have given us some of the most memorable and critically acclaimed films of recent years.” 

	Harris is best-known for her longstanding partnership with Sam Mendes, with whom she co-founded Neal Street Productions. Alongside Oscar and BAFTA winners “Hamnet” and “1917,” her film credits including “Revolutionary Road,” “Jarhead” and recent family feature “The Magic Faraway Tree,” while on TV her productions include “Call the Midwife,” “Penny Dreadful” and “Britannia.”

	Wilson, meanwhile, has an ongoing collaboration with director Jonathan Glazer, with whom he’s worked on both the Oscar and BAFTA-winning “The Zone of Interest” and “Under the Skin.” Last year, he produced Kaouther Ben Hania’s Oscar-nominated “The Voice of Hind Rajab,” while his other credits include Lynne Ramsay’s “You Were Never Really Here,” Aneil Karia’s “Hamlet” and “20,000 Days on Earth,” directed by  Iain Forsyth and Jane Pollard.
	

	The full LFF industry forum programme will be announced mid- September. The festival runs Oct 7-18.

schema.headline: Pippa Harris and James Wilson to Headline London Film Festival Industry Forum

title: Netflix Sets ‘Ad Vitam’ Sequel With Guillaume Canet
description:
Netflix has started production on a sequel to “Ad Vitam,” its 2025 French action thriller starring Guillaume Canet.

	The sequel has the working tit
body:
Netflix has started production on a sequel to “Ad Vitam,” its 2025 French action thriller starring Guillaume Canet.

	The sequel has the working title “Ad Vitam Eternam,” which is Latin for “to eternal life.” Canet is returning as Franck Lazareff, a former operator for the GIGN, the elite tactical unit of the French National Gendarmerie. 

	“After surviving an assassination attempt upon his release from prison, Franck sets out to find out who wants him dead,” the sequel’s synopsis reads. “He goes to hide away with his family in the mountains. But French intelligence services track him down and offer him a deal: a covert mission in exchange for the truth Franck is seeking.”
	

	The “Ad Vitam” sequel will be directed by Ludovic Colbeau-Justin (“Néro: The Assassin”), replacing the original film’s helmer Rodolphe Lauga. The screenplay was penned by Canet and French novelist Maxime Chattam with the collaboration of David Corona, who co-wrote the first movie’s script. 


	Alongside Canet, “Ad Vitam Eternam” will star Stéphane Caillard, Nassim Lyes, Zita Hanrot, Nicolas Duvauchelle,  Sophie Marceau and Mathieu Amalric. It’s produced by Canet and Jean Cottin for their Cabanes Productions and will shoot in locations around France including Ile-de-France, Normandy, Savoie and Provence-Alpes-Côte d’Azur.

	The first “Ad Vitam” movie was a hit for Netflix France and climbed to No. 9 on the streamer’s most popular non-English film chart. “Ad Vitam Eternam” joins a robust Netflix France slate which includes “Call My Agent: The Movie” on Sept. 10, “Lupin” Season 4 on Oct. 23 and “Quasimodo” starring Vincent Cassel.

schema.headline: Netflix Sets ‘Ad Vitam’ Sequel With Guillaume Canet

title: How Norway’s Øyafestivalen Became One of Europe’s Best Music Fests: Balancing Huge Headliners With Homegrown Artists, Prioritizing Gender Parity and More
description: In a year without Glastonbury, music lovers have turned to other festivals in the U.K. and Europe to fill the void. There’s Primavera Sound in Barce
body:
In a year without Glastonbury, music lovers have turned to other festivals in the U.K. and Europe to fill the void. There’s Primavera Sound in Barcelona, with its proximity to the beach and genre-diverse lineup, or Reading and Leeds in England for those who want a true camping experience with a rock-focused flair. But look a little further north and you’ll find a hidden gem that’s capturing the attention of both festivalgoers and artists around the world: Øyafestivalen in Oslo, Norway.
	

	Compared to a juggernaut festival like Glasto — known for its sprawling grounds, mandatory camping and rowdy atmosphere — Øya, which kicks off on Wednesday, delivers a more intimate experience. The capacity is about 10 times less (with 22,000 people expected to attend each day this year), it’s held in Tøyen Park in the middle of Oslo and there’s a certain Scandinavian politeness that seems to keep people from getting completely off their faces. But over the past decade or so, Øya has consistently delivered huge headliners and some of the best, most varied lineup curation on the festival scene, booking everyone from Blur to Kendrick Lamar to Charli xcx.


	This year’s four-day lineup is headlined by the Cure, Nick Cave and the Bad Seeds, Sombr and homegrown artist Dagny, but also includes Geese, Wilco, Lily Allen, Clipse, Blood Orange and Tomora (the collaboration between Chemical Brothers’ Tom Rowlands and Norwegian singer Aurora). There’s truly something for everyone, and its relatively small capacity, lack of huge crowds and overall peaceful vibe make it possible to actually see the artist you’re watching.
	

	“Everybody can book a big headliner and put on a big show, but it’s the details and taking care of everything — being really nerdy on where you put the toilets and the bars and the sound bleed between the stages — all these things are very important,” says Claes Olsen, who co-founded the festival in 1999 and serves as its booking manager. “That’s what makes it unique.”

	It’s such an enjoyable experience for artists and attendees alike that many of them — like the Cure, Nick Cave, Wilco and Blood Orange this year — are repeat bookings. As its profile has grown worldwide, Olsen says artist requests to play the festival have increased as well. Nowadays, Øya books its lineup up to 17 months in advance.

	“We’re getting tons [of requests] every day,” Olsen says. “So as a booker, one of the most important jobs we actually do is to say no to people, which is not that fun. It’s hard. But of course, we also have to reach out a lot.” 

	Something Olsen is particularly proud of is that the Cure — who previously headlined the fest in 2019 — asked to come back before the band plans to retire in 2029. “We got an email from the agent for the Cure saying that Robert Smith wanted to play Øya before they stopped being the Cure,” he says. “I’ve been a fan since I was a teenager, so that was pretty amazing.”



	

					Robert Smith from the Cure at Øya Fest in 2019.
									Redferns
	



	But it’s not just about attracting acts from the U.K. and U.S. for Øya — the festival puts a huge emphasis on local Norwegian artists, mixing them in throughout each day so it’s “not just them playing first and hoping somebody shows up,” Olsen says. And, the headlining spot on Saturday, the final day of the festival, always goes to a homegrown artist. This year, it’s dance-pop singer Dagny (pictured above), who hails from the city of Tromsø and broke through with hits like “Somebody” and “Drink About.”

	For Dagny, headlining Øya has always been a dream, ever since she first played on a small stage at the festival a decade ago. “It’s kind of my Madison Square Garden, if you know what I mean,” she says. “Øya is one of those festivals where I feel like people are so open to music and to just being present, right there and then in the crowd. It’s really one of my favorites.” 

	She just released her third album, “Dancefloor Erotica,” which leans more into electro-pop and marks a real creative milestone in her career. “I feel weirdly out of my comfort zone, but at the same time I feel like I’m where I want to be,” Dagny says. “We have such a different energy now playing this record — it’s a bit darker, it’s a bit heavier, a bit more danceable.”
	

	Another priority for Øya is gender parity, with the festival committing to a roughly even split between male and female performers. This year, Saturday’s main stage lineup is only women, headlined by Dagny but also including Lily Allen, Irish breakout CMAT and U.S. singer Hannah Cohen.

	“Øya is real proof that [gender parity] doesn’t have to be a problem because they’re probably the biggest Norwegian festival and they always seem to get a pretty even balance,” Dagny says. “Not only am I the headliner on that stage with lots of female artists that day, but I think I’m also something like the fifth or sixth female artist to headline that slot in the last few years.”

	This was of the utmost importance to U.K.-based feminist band Girl Group — four out of five members of which hail from Oslo — who are playing Øya for the first time. Having formed at the Liverpool Institute for the Performing Arts in response to the male-dominated culture they experienced, Girl Group only works with women and nonbinary people, from the music-making process down to their videos and photography.

	“They care a lot about the environment and feminism, and they try to make active choices for society, not just the festival itself,” Girl Group’s Mia Halvorsen says of Øya. “For us, being on a lineup with all the women we really value feels very special and meaningful. And obviously, our project is very political and very feminist, so it feels good to be seeing a bit more of that in festivals.”



	

					Girl Group
									Serskaten
	



	In addition to its gender split pledge, Øya is a leader in festival sustainability, prioritizing waste management, stopping the use of fuel generators in 2008, and only serving meat-free food since 2024. Last year, the fest added human rights to this initiative, and is once again partnering with Amnesty International to fundraise for medical aid in Palestine.

	“Working with Amnesty has helped us a lot to educate ourselves on the whole human rights situation, not only in Palestine but other places in the world as well,” Olsen says. “That work is super important going forward.”

	As Øya has grown on the global stage, Norway as a whole has been experiencing a bit of a cultural moment. From Joachim Trier’s “Sentimental Value” bringing the country its first international feature Oscar earlier this year to their football team making it to the World Cup semi-finals, Norway’s profile is rapidly rising.
	

	“It’s good to see Norwegian people charming the world a bit,” Olsen says. “It’s been really hard groundwork for the last 10 years, so I hope that continues.”

	Dagny has not only observed an uptick in Norwegian artists being recognized internationally, but also on a local scale. “Music in the mother tongue has completely gone up,” she says. “I think after COVID, it’s pretty much just been Norwegian music that has been happening in Norway, with a few exceptions. Seeing how many Norwegian artists are doing so great, it’s helping to raise everyone’s bar of where we’re going to be at.”

	Having lived in the U.K. for nearly a decade before moving back to Oslo before the pandemic, Dagny also believes that Norway’s environment contributes to her creative output. “Norway is thankfully a small and peaceful place, and sometimes what you need to be creative is time and space and quiet,” she says. “I think there is maybe something to the fact that I didn’t write an album until I moved back to Norway.” 

	Girl Group, who are currently based in Liverpool, have come to a similar realization — though for them, the artistic freedom they feel in Norway can be traced back to the way the country is run. 

	“We are a socialist country, we pay taxes, we have good education,” says Girl Group’s Katya Birkeland. “When you have good education, you get good directors, people who get to do acting, people who get to spend their time practicing football — you get people who get to do what they love.”

	Adds member Maria Tollisen, “I think you need to be privileged and have a bit of financial safety and stability in order to be able to do art.” 

	Beyond just spotlighting homegrown acts, Øya also serves as a bit of a reunion for the local scene. “If you’re in a certain music scene in Oslo, it’s almost impossible to not have met a lot of [the acts],” Dagny says, mentioning that she’s looking forward to catching up-and-coming artist Ary and Tomora at the festival.

	Girl Group also mentions Ary as a must-see artist, as well as the band Three40Four and singer-songwriters Elia and Ea Othilde. “One of my childhood best friends is a dancer for [Ary] now and I’ve not seen her for ages,” Birkeland says. “I can’t wait!”

schema.headline: How Norway’s Øyafestivalen Became One of Europe’s Best Music Fests: Balancing Huge Headliners With Homegrown Artists, Prioritizing Gender Parity and More

title: Latin Quarter Distribution Acquires World Rights to José Dell’Acqua Uruguayan Crime Thriller ‘Maltrato Animal’ (EXCLUSIVE)
description:
Latin Quarter Distribution has acquired world sales rights to José Dell’Acqua’s Uruguayan crime thriller “Maltrato Animal” (“Animal Budget”). 

	The
body:
Latin Quarter Distribution has acquired world sales rights to José Dell’Acqua’s Uruguayan crime thriller “Maltrato Animal” (“Animal Budget”). 

	The deal was closed after a screening of “Maltrato Animal” at Locarno’s First Look, a pix-in-post competition focused on rough-cut screenings of emerging and established talent from a territory around the world, this year Uruguay.  

	Presented in Locarno by the Agencia del Cine y el Audiovisual del Uruguay (ACAU), which is still building Uruguay’s film-TV ecosysytem, the film, currently in the editing stage, is set against the backdrop of Uruguay’s 2002 economic crisis and explores a generation shaped by that pivotal moment in the country’s history. 
	

	Bankrupted by the financial crisis, a Montevideo veterinarian is pushed to desperate straits and doesn’t have enough money to eat. In order to survive, he enters a clandestine network of illegal breeding operations and pharmaceutical peddling. In this downward spiral, an unexpected encounter potentially opens a new chapter in his life.


	Produced by Dell’Acqua and German Ormaechea, the film was shot over a four-year period — one week each year — with the support of numerous Uruguayan technicians and rental companies. The project brought together many first-time department heads, including cinematographer Germán Couto and costume designer Victoria Zavaleta, as well as an entirely Uruguayan cast, according to Dell’Aqua. Developed over eight years, the film blends fiction and reality to portray a deeply personal and collective memory. 

	“‘Maltrato Animal’ was born from the need to revisit the generation that grew up during Uruguay’s 2002 economic crisis,” Dell’Acqua said. “Over eight years, I wrote, directed, and produced the film, seeking to blur the boundaries between fiction and reality. It is also a celebration of the talent of a new generation of Uruguayan filmmakers, many of whom took on leading creative roles in their first feature film.” 
	

	“After such a long and personal journey with ‘Maltrato Animal,’ I’m very happy to begin this next stage with Latin Quarter Distribution,” Dell’Aqua told Variety. “Their bold approach and distinctive curation feel deeply aligned with the spirit of the film. I believe they understand the kind of cinema we are trying to make and, most importantly, have the commitment and passion to bring it to audiences beyond Uruguay.” 

	Juan G. Castro, founder and managing director of The Hague-based Latin Quarter Distribution, added:  “We’re excited to add ‘Maltrato Animal’ to the Latin Quarter slate. We’re always searching for new gems and distinctive voices in Latin American arthouse cinema, and José Dell’Acqua’s first feature immediately stood out to us. Discovering the film through ACAU’s presentation of Uruguayan cinema at Locarno makes this acquisition particularly meaningful, and we’re proud to support a film that showcases the talent and originality emerging from Uruguay today.” 

	Post-production on “Maltrato Animal” is expected to be completed by the end of 2026.

schema.headline: Latin Quarter Distribution Acquires World Rights to José Dell’Acqua Uruguayan Crime Thriller ‘Maltrato Animal’ (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Alessandra Sanguinetti on Her Dreamy, Grounded Directorial Debut ‘The Illusion of an Everlasting Summer’
description: In the Argentine Pampas, cousins Guillermina and Belinda cannot wait to grow up. When they are not swimming in the river and dancing through the lon
body:
In the Argentine Pampas, cousins Guillermina and Belinda cannot wait to grow up. When they are not swimming in the river and dancing through the long, breezy afternoons, they re-enact funeral ceremonies and feign surgery on dead animals. This quotidian desire to accelerate the inevitable passing of time animates photographer Alessandra Sanguinetti’s debut feature, “The Illusion of an Everlasting Summer.”  

	Presented in world premiere in Filmmakers of the Present at the 79th edition of the Locarno Film Festival, the film was produced by distinguished director-producer Julia Solomonoff (“Nobody’s Watching”), with financing from Mubi and Impact Partners. 
	

	Sanguinetti’s gaze follows Guille and Belinda while they grow up, fall in love, raise children and slowly drift toward separate lives over two and a half decades. The seemingly home-footage structure forms a familiar and intimate setting, in which the grainy footage narrates the life passing between the moments Sanguinetti captured as part of her extensive, decades-long photography of close cousins Guille and Belinda. 


	“We’re just like extended family now,” says the director about her relationship with the duo, spanning over 25 years. “It was really organic. I did not want to make a project about two women growing up. I just knew them and wanted to be with them.” 

	Static framing and pixelated vignettes of tranquil farmland in Sanguinetti’s work trace back to formal similarities to “Dry Leaf,” directed by Alexandre Koberidze, another Locarno title, screened in 2025. The Argentinian prairie is adorned with imaginary houses, castles and theatres as the young girls construct spontaneous, invisible cities, stories and games in which Koberidze’s likewise unseen characters could live. Lively farm animals populate the backgrounds against which Guille and Belinda confidently perform their silly and earnest singing and dancing.
	

	Although the result bears some resemblance, the two directors employ the graininess for different aesthetic reasons. In Sanguinetti’s practice, the video camera appeared as a natural prop that watched and filmed Belinda and Guille’s performances while the director captured with her photographic camera “what happens slowly in the moment.” Comparing photography to video, she says about her relationship with the first, “I’m always more in control and looking for something. With video, I could let life flow in front of me and then later think about what to retrieve or not.”

	These snapshots of life, then overlooked as common moments, might be actually foundational to one’s trajectory, as “we don’t realize that we’re defining ourselves in that moment. You can only see that when you’re at a certain distance, when you’re knowing and loving them, but you’re not being their mother.” This in turn enabled Sanguinetti to observe “patterns in the girls’ lives — what kept repeating or changing, what things they had escaped from, and what they achieved through sheer will.”

	Sanguinetti’s tender film detours through the motions of time and eventually brings fleshiness to her presence. “In the beginning, I didn’t want to be a part of it. I thought my voice would ruin it. As the time went by, I realized that I was there and I just had to accept it.”

	If women constitute the film’s heart, animals form its pulse. Neither pets nor crude products of an economy, Sanguinetti deftly places cattle, dogs and cats alongside people and land. Essential to the farmland Pampas, the girls’ grandmother repeatedly confesses to the director about the joy of taking care of chickens and their innate beauty or the bovines’ way of behaving as a tightly knit community. 

	This sentiment is personal for Sanguinetti: “I’ve always considered animals equal to humans,” adding on their importance to the rural ecosystem: “I always felt that the animals in that space were ignored. But these people are here because of the animals in that area, because there is no agriculture.”

schema.headline: Alessandra Sanguinetti on Her Dreamy, Grounded Directorial Debut ‘The Illusion of an Everlasting Summer’

title: ‘Brave New Love’ Review: Infidelity Isn’t the End in an Unusual, Open-Minded Marital Drama
description: “I would never fall in love if I was in a good relationship.” So says one participant in the women’s church group where Copenhagen-based wife and mo
body:
“I would never fall in love if I was in a good relationship.” So says one participant in the women’s church group where Copenhagen-based wife and mother Kate (Kathrine Thorborg Johansen) confesses that she’s been having a three-year affair with another man, and doesn’t much regret it. It’s a line that sounds like sturdy, suitably Christian advice, but is it true? Kate’s husband Orla (Simon Sears) is attentive, attractive and empathetic; so is Andreas (Anders Danielsen Lie), the smart, offbeat archaeologist she’s smitten with at first sight. Alternately droll and emotionally acute, Maria Bäck’s “Brave New Love” never presents this romantic triangle as a problem with one solution; it’s considerably less judgmental than the church ladies as it gives its protagonist space to figure out if she really loves two people at once, or just loves nobody — herself included — quite enough.
	

	Premiering in the main competition at Locarno, this is an emotionally intelligent, gently wry character drama of a distinctly Scandi stripe, occupying a comparable arthouse lane to Dag Johan Haugerud’s Oslo Trilogy and recent works by Joachim Trier, albeit with a distinctly feminine point of view behind the camera. It’s not just Danielsen Lie’s reliably interesting presence that brings to mind “The Worst Person in the World” at points, as Bäck’s script (on which Trier collaborator Eskil Vogt was a consultant) ponders similar feelings of middle-class millennial female unrest in a character who simply opted for marriage and family earlier in life. Relatable and discussable, Bäck’s second narrative feature likely reps an easier sell to international distributors than her first, the darkly heightened psychodrama “Psychosis in Stockholm.”
	

	It’s on a camping trip with her family that Kate first locks eyes with Andreas — they’re both stark naked, having just swum in the same forest lake, but that’s rendered almost incidental by the telling intensity of their shared gaze. When he walks off, Kate scribbles down her number and leaves it under his towel. But then “Brave New Love” takes the first of several swerves: Instead of charting its protagonist’s first steps into infidelity, it skips breezily through snapshots from the ensuing years-long affair. Andreas becomes almost as entrenched a partner in her life as her husband, though she manages to keep the relationships strictly separate — a rationalized arrangement in her mind, though that collapses when Andreas calmly announces that he’s moving to Greece for a job.

	It’s only with the affair on ice that disorder creeps into Kate’s life, while Orla and their teenage daughter Athena (an excellent Noemi Carbone Mannov) begin to sense something amiss. Editor Julius Krebs Damsbo artfully toggles between present and past, gradually filling in the sensual specifics of the affair — which aren’t entirely as you’d expect — while tracking Kate’s spiraling sense of mourning for whatever it was they had. Without it, her comfortable marriage to Orla seems that much more confined, the increasingly separate islands they seem to be on underlined by DP Maria Von Hausswolff in one tense bedtime argument scene, with the couple’s faces visible only in their respective bathroom-vanity mirrors. Kate seeks solidarity in the aforementioned church group, despite not being much of a believer herself; she doesn’t quite find it, but the candor enabled by all-female company is its own kind of liberation.

	Thorborg Johansen’s subtly nervy performance articulates Kate’s antsy anxieties and erratic moods without making her too much of a scatty romantic heroine. She’s believable while not straining too hard for our sympathy, which winds up fairly evenly divided between all the principals anyway — with a slight advantage to Sears’ beautifully modulated turn as Orla, battling his own emotional and bodily securities while trying to hold down the fort. Handed the most script’s least knowable character, Andersen Lie nonetheless sharply gestures to a life outside his relations with Kate, something she herself hasn’t much considered. In its efforts to be fair to all these characters — via a key, spirit-lightening change of scene — “Brave New Love’s” final act winds up a little fuzzy, though that’s a preferable flaw to tunnel vision: Bäck’s film prefers untidy personal drama to a tidy moral verdict.

title: Sadhguru, Graphic India Team on Animated Epic ‘Shiva: The Adiyogi’ (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Indian yogi and mystic Sadhguru is teaming with Graphic India on “Shiva: The Adiyogi,” an animated feature retelling the origin story of Hindu God S
body:
Indian yogi and mystic Sadhguru is teaming with Graphic India on “Shiva: The Adiyogi,” an animated feature retelling the origin story of Hindu God Shiva as the first yogi. 

	Sadhguru and Sharad Devarajan share story credit on the film.

	Graphic India is the studio behind India’s animated mythology franchise “The Legend of Hanuman.” Devarajan, who co-created that series and co-founded Graphic India, is producing, co-writing and co-creating “Shiva: The Adiyogi.”
	

	The film spans from before creation to the peaks of Kailash, taking in the rage of Veerabhadra, a being formed from grief, and the devotion of two women whose bond keeps Shiva connected to existence. It builds to a scene at Kanti Sarovar in which Shiva imparts 112 methods for transcending physical existence to seven seekers.


	“In the yogic culture, Shiva is not seen as a God. For us, Shiva is the Adiyogi – the first yogi, and the Adiguru – the first guru. For the first time in the history of humanity, Shiva the Adiyogi introduced the idea that the simple laws of nature are not permanent restrictions. If one is willing to strive, one can go beyond all limitations and attain to liberation. Breaking the laws of physical nature is spiritual process. In this sense, we are outlaws, and Shiva is the ultimate outlaw,” said Sadhguru.

	“This is the story of how wisdom itself was born, and why it was shared with humanity,” added Devarajan. “As a storyteller, there is no greater canvas, a cosmic love story, a tale of devastating loss, and action on a scale no epic has ever attempted. Armies of gods fall before a warrior born of pure grief. A blind conqueror storms the gates of heaven. A third eye opens and burns desire itself out of existence. And through all the fury and spectacle runs the most tender story imaginable, of the two women whose love was fierce enough to reach an infinite being, and the final gift he gave humanity because of them. To craft this story alongside Sadhguru, the defining voice of the Adiyogi in our time, is the greatest creative honor I could imagine.”
	

	Sadhguru is also a bestselling author whose videos stream in 35 languages on social media. He founded the Isha Foundation, a nonprofit human-service organization, more than three decades ago; it is now supported by over 19 million volunteers worldwide.

	Devarajan’s credits also include the “Baahubali” animated series, comprising “Baahubali: The Lost Legends” and “Baahubali: Crown of Blood,” and the co-creation of Pavitr Prabhakar, the Indian Spider-Man character for Marvel who appeared in the Oscar-nominated “Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse.”

	“Shiva: The Adiyogi” is targeting a worldwide theatrical release. Jeevan J. Kang and Subrah S. Iyar serve as executive producers and Navin Miranda and Nayana Bijli as co-producers. Production is being led by Graphic India’s animation studio.

title: In-N-Out Sued for Religious Discrimination, Wrongful Termination
description:
In-N-Out Sued
                          YOU'RE NOT AS CHRISTIAN AS YOU SAY YOU ARE!!!
body:
In-N-Out Sued
                          YOU'RE NOT AS CHRISTIAN AS YOU SAY YOU ARE!!!
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              August 10, 2026
                            1:00 AM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  August 10, 2026
                                5:49 AM PDT
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            In-N-Out is being grilled with a religious discrimination lawsuit ... a former cook says the company treated her differently and ultimately fired her after she asked for a different work schedule due to her Christian beliefs.
      
    
            According to the suit, obtained by TMZ, Arianna Rodriguez said she had been working as a cook for the burger chain's Long Beach, CA location for nearly 5 years without issues with a schedule that allowed her to attend church on Sundays.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            She claims this wasn't an issue until a new manager started in October. She alleges her Sunday availability then became a "recurring source of workplace conflict," and she got her first-ever write-up during this time.
      

            In December, she claims she went to upper-level management, claiming she had concerns about her availability, church attendance, and unfair treatment … but said her concerns were dismissed.
      
    
            Then on June 24, Arianna claims "an incident occurred involving food" that she thought was "waste under the workplace practice she had observed" … but she says In-N-Out reported her to HR, suspended her, and began investigating the incident.
      
    
      
        
              
    
    
            It's unclear what the incident was, but the cook claims other employees have done something similar and weren't suspended or fired … only received warnings.
      
    
            According to the lawsuit, she went to HR to complain about the "unequal treatment" but says she was then fired on July 3 for an alleged policy violation.
      
    
            She's now suing for religious discrimination, wrongful termination, and more. She's asking for unspecified damages, unpaid wages, and to get her job back.

title: 'A Christmas Story' Actress Tedde Moore Dead at 79
description:
'A Christmas Story' Tedde Moore
                          Dead At 79
body:
'A Christmas Story' Tedde Moore
                          Dead At 79
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              August 10, 2026
                            4:04 AM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  August 10, 2026
                                5:24 AM PDT
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Actress Tedde Moore -- who famously played Miss Shields in "A Christmas Story" — has died.
      
    
            Moore passed away last Wednesday in Huntsville, Ontario, Canada, according to a Facebook post under her name. Her cause of death was not released.
      
    
            Moore kicked off her acting career by starring alongside Christopher Walken in the play, "A Midsummer Night's Dream," in Stratford, Ontario. 
      

            She then landed her biggest role as Miss Shields in the hit 1983 film, "A Christmas Story." Moore was unforgettable as the uber-strict teacher of 9-year-old Ralphie Parker, played by Peter Billingsley.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Moore also secured roles in other films, such as "Second Wind," "Murder by Decree," "Overnight," and "Down the Road Again."
      
    
            Her credits on the small screen included the TV movie, "Mistletoe over Manhattan," and the mini-series, "The Kennedys."
      
    
            Moore was 79.
      
    
            RIP

description:

                          The Diaspora's Calling ...
                          Huge S
body:
Lauryn Hill
                          The Diaspora's Calling ...
                          Huge Stars Answer!!!
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              August 9, 2026
                            5:38 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
            Lauryn Hill's Diaspora Calling! festival rang some big stars ... and they answered -- rocking a crowd of 35,000 in the United Kingdom on Friday.
      
    
            The singer-songwriter's event took place at The National Bowl in Milton Keynes, England ... and hosted by Dave Chappelle -- who has got a ton of experience working a crowd.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Hill -- who conceived the event to celebrate Africa and its global diaspora -- took the stage of course ... and was joined by Erykah Badu. Together, the pair played the track "Doo Wop (That Thing).”
      

            Zion Marley took the stage and paid tribute to his grandfather -- Bob Marley -- by singing his famous track "Three Little Birds."
      
    
            Kano and Giggs -- two of the biggest voices in British rap these days -- joined each other during the show ... and Hill and Wyclef Jean collaborated to celebrate the 30th anniversary of The Fugees’ album "The Score."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            While the performers were massive stars, so were several members of the audience ... with Gunna, Common, Rapsody and many more stars spotted attending.
      
    
            And, like we said, 35K people heard the diaspora's call and headed to the stadium ... a pretty impressive audience size.
      
    
            Usually, Lauryn Hill's killing us softly ... but there was nothing quiety about this event!

title: Aubrey Plaza Welcomes First Child With Christopher Abbott
body:

            Aubrey Plaza is officially a mom ... welcoming her first child with partner Christopher Abbott!
      
    
            Aubrey was seen holding her little bundle of joy on Sunday in New York City after seeing "Death of a Salesman" -- Chris' last performance.
      
    
            Sources with direct knowledge tell TMZ … Aubrey welcomed a baby girl during the last week of July, making the couple a family of three.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Aubrey looking effortless in a high ponytail and chic black sunglasses. Their baby was wrapped snugly in a blanket and beanie … cozied up in the first-time mom’s arms.
      

                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            As we reported ... news of Aubrey's pregnancy surfaced in April, with the baby expected to arrive in the fall.
      
    
            The 'White Lotus' star made no effort to hide her growing belly in the months that followed ... stepping out with her bump on display as she prepared to become a first-time mom.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The new arrival marks Aubrey and Christopher's first child together. She was previously married to screenwriter and director Jeff Baena, but they did not have children before their separation and his death.
      
    
            Aubrey and Christopher previously worked together on the 2020 movie "Black Bear" and the off-Broadway play "Danny and the Deep Blue Sea."
      
    
            Congrats to the new parents!!!
